faq.q: Will this teach me to hack?
faq.a: No. The course is defensive and teaches everyday protection. It does not teach attacking systems, and it reminds learners that accessing systems without permission is illegal.
No. It is written for everyday users, with a little arithmetic in the password lab.

faq.q: Is it a professional security certification?
faq.a: No. It gives a foundation in cyber safety, but it is not an externally accredited security certification.

activities.title: Why password length matters
activities.objective: Compare how many guesses different passwords need and how long an attacker might take.
activities.scenario: An attacker's computer can try 1,000,000,000 (one billion) guesses a second against a leaked, weakly protected password file. Compare how many guesses are possible for different passwords.
steps: In D2 work out the number of possible passwords: the character set size (B) raised to the length (C) using POWER.
Fill down to D6.
In E2 work out the seconds to try them all: D2 divided by the guesses per second in B9 (lock B9).
In F2 convert to days: E2 divided by 86400. Fill E and F down.
In B11 show Weak if the days needed are below 1, otherwise Better, for the first row using IF.

checks.label: D2 is the number of possibilities for the first password
checks.hint: =POWER(B2,C2)
checks.explain: Set size raised to the length.

checks.label: D6 is filled
checks.hint: Fill down.
checks.explain: The same rule for each row.

checks.label: E2 is seconds to try all
checks.explain: Possibilities divided by guesses per second.

checks.label: F4 is days for row 4
checks.explain: Seconds divided by 86,400 in a day.

checks.label: F6 shows the long password takes far longer
checks.hint: Fill down.

checks.label: B11 is the verdict
checks.hint: =IF(F2<1,"Weak","Better")
checks.explain: Under a day to try everything is weak.

activities.title: Report a suspicious email
activities.objective: Write a clear report to the IT security team.
activities.scenario: You received a suspicious email pretending to be the college accounts office asking you to confirm your login. You did not click anything. Write the report.
steps: Write a subject line starting with Subject:.
Say what you received, when and from which address (invent plausible details).
Say what you did and did not do (for example, you did not click the link).
Ask what to do next and say you will delete it only after they reply.
Keep it under 130 words.

checks.label: A subject line
checks.hint: Begin with Subject:.

checks.label: Describes the email
checks.hint: Mention the sender and the request.

checks.label: States that you did not click
checks.hint: Say you did not click.
checks.explain: It tells the team the risk level.

checks.label: Asks what to do next
checks.hint: Ask for advice.

checks.label: Between 40 and 130 words
checks.hint: Short and clear.
checks.explain: Reports should be quick to read.

activities.title: Plan a 3-2-1 backup
activities.objective: Check that a backup plan keeps enough copies in enough places and estimate storage.
activities.scenario: Follow the 3-2-1 rule: at least 3 copies, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site. Check a student's plan and estimate storage needed.
steps: In B8 count the copies with COUNTA on column A (rows 2 to 6).
In B9 count the off-site copies with COUNTIF on column C for the text Yes.
In B10 total the data size in GB for all copies with SUM on column B.
In B11 show Meets 3-2-1 if there are at least 3 copies and at least 1 off-site, using IF and AND.

checks.label: B8 counts the copies
checks.hint: =COUNTA(A2:A6)

checks.label: B9 counts off-site copies
checks.hint: =COUNTIF(C2:C6,"Yes")

checks.label: B10 totals the storage
checks.hint: =SUM(B2:B6)

checks.label: B11 is the verdict
checks.hint: =IF(AND(B8>=3,B9>=1),"Meets 3-2-1","Improve")

activities.title: Build a personal risk register
activities.objective: Score security risks by likelihood and impact and rank what to fix first.
activities.scenario: A student listed five risks to their digital life. Score each and see which to fix first.
steps: In D2 enter likelihood times impact (both 1 to 5). Fill down to D6.
In E2 show Fix now if the score is 15 or more, Plan if 8 or more, otherwise Watch (nested IF). Fill down.
In B8 find the highest score with MAX.
In B9 count how many risks are Fix now with COUNTIF.

checks.label: D2 is likelihood times impact
D6 is filled
checks.hint: Fill down.

checks.label: E2 is Fix now
checks.hint: =IF(D2>=15,"Fix now",IF(D2>=8,"Plan","Watch"))
checks.explain: A nested IF gives three levels.

checks.label: E6 is Watch
checks.hint: Fill down.

checks.label: B8 is the highest score
checks.hint: =MAX(D2:D6)

checks.label: B9 counts Fix now risks
checks.hint: =COUNTIF(E2:E6,"Fix now")

activities.title: Write an incident response checklist
activities.objective: Write the first steps to take when you think an account has been hacked.
activities.scenario: You get an alert that someone logged in to your email from another country. Write your own response plan.
steps: Add a Heading 1 'If my account is hacked'.
Add Heading 2 sections: Stop the damage, Recover, Tell people, Learn.
Under each, write a numbered list of at least two steps.
Include changing the password, turning on two-step verification and checking recovery settings.
Keep it between 100 and 260 words.

checks.label: A title
checks.hint: Use Heading 1.

checks.label: Four sections
checks.hint: Use Heading 2.

checks.label: Sections in order
checks.hint: Stop the damage, Recover, Tell people, Learn.

checks.label: Numbered steps
checks.hint: Use the numbered list button.

checks.label: Mentions changing the password
checks.hint: Include change password.

checks.label: Mentions two-step verification
checks.hint: Include two-step or two-factor.
checks.explain: A second check stops repeat access.

checks.label: Between 100 and 260 words
checks.hint: Concise.
checks.explain: A checklist must be quick to follow.

activities.title: Final project: a personal security plan
activities.objective: Combine accounts, devices, data, privacy and incident response into one practical plan.
activities.scenario: Write a one-page security plan for yourself or for a family member who is new to smartphones.
steps: Add a Heading 1 'My security plan'.
Add Heading 2 sections: Accounts, Devices, Data and backups, Spotting scams, If something goes wrong.
Under each section write a bulleted list of at least two actions.
Include one number somewhere (for example a backup frequency or password length).
Keep it between 150 and 340 words.
